title: A hundred and five years: Dattopant Thengadi's birth anniversary
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Born on Deepawali, 10 November 1920. Ten ideas to carry forward.
body:
*Photo: Dattopant Thengadi*

**10 November 2025** marked 105 years since the birth of **Dattopant Thengadi** in Arvi, a town in the Wardha district of Maharashtra, in 1920. A birth anniversary is a good occasion to ask what a thinker has left that can still be used. Below are ten of his ideas that remain useful for a trade union worker today, each with a short explanation of what it means in practice.

## The man behind the ideas

Thengadi studied at Morris College and took his law degree at the Law College in Nagpur. He became a full-time RSS pracharak and spent years working in different parts of the country, including Kerala, Bengal and Assam. He was a member of the Rajya Sabha from 1964 to 1976 and wrote on economics, labour, society and philosophy in Hindi, English and Marathi. His books include *The Third Way*, *Modernization without Westernization* and *The Perspective*. He founded the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh on 23 July 1955 and later helped create the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh, the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch and other bodies. He owned no property and sought no honours; he declined a national award that was offered to him in 2003.

## Ten ideas that remain useful

**1. Nation first.** BMS speaks of three interests in a fixed order of concern: the nation, the industry and the worker. The idea is not that the worker is unimportant, but that no lasting gain for workers can come from harming the country's economy or security. In practice it explains why BMS has backed the government in times of national emergency and has opposed it when workers' interests have been ignored; Thengadi called this approach "responsive cooperation", meaning cooperation or non-cooperation depending on how workers are treated.

**2. Constructive trade unionism.** Be firm in demands but constructive in method. A BMS union prepares its charter of demands, presents it, negotiates and, if all else fails, agitates peacefully. It does not use violence or destruction of property as a method.

**3. Class cooperation, not class conflict.** Employers and workers are partners in a common task and share a common interest in the survival of the enterprise. Thengadi proposed the **Udyog Parivar**, the "industrial family", as an Indian alternative to both the master-servant model and class struggle. He also suggested that the Industrial Disputes Act should be renamed the Industrial Relations Act, so that the law's very name would speak of relations and not of disputes. This does not mean that a union should accept every employer decision. A family is not one in which the junior members are silent; it is one in which each member is heard.

**4. Labourisation.** Thengadi's slogan was to give labour the standing that capital normally has. Workers are not just a cost; their labour is itself a form of capital, and it deserves a share in the profits and in decisions. One writer on the BMS describes the idea as treating workers as shareholders in the enterprise. A related position is that bonus is deferred wages, that is, a part of wages that is postponed and not a gift from the employer.

**5. Workers unite the world.** In place of the slogan that calls on workers of the world to unite in opposition to others, BMS holds that workers should unite the world, in the sense that they are the builders and not the destroyers. This is a statement about method as well as ideology: the worker's strength is used for construction.

**6. Vishwakarma Jayanti.** BMS marks **Vishwakarma Jayanti, on 17 September**, as its labour day. The date is fixed for uniformity, since the festival is observed on different lunar dates in different regions. BMS regards 1 May as a day tied to a foreign movement and prefers a day that comes from India's own tradition of respecting the craftsman and the builder.

**7. The Vishwakarma sector.** The artisan, the self-employed worker and the small producer do not fit neatly into the old picture of an employer and an employee. Thengadi insisted that they should be recognised, supported and given social security. This idea is closer than ever to the present, when much of the country's workforce is self-employed or in informal work and when the Government is working to extend social security to unorganised and platform workers.

**8. Swadeshi.** Producers in the country should come first and trade should be on fair terms. Swadeshi does not mean a closed economy; it means that the country should not be reduced to a market for others and that its farmers, artisans and small industries should not be destroyed in the name of competition. The Swadeshi Jagaran Manch, which he founded in 1991, was created to argue this case when the economy was being opened up.

**9. Consumer sovereignty.** The buyer must not be helpless. Thengadi took part in forming the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat, a consumers' organisation, and argued that industrial settlements should take into account the interests of consumers too. A union that pushes for higher wages while ignoring the price and quality of what is produced is, in his view, incomplete.

**10. Social harmony.** *Samarasata*, the feeling of belonging together, is the base of any lasting movement. He was close to Dr B. R. Ambedkar during the last years of Ambedkar's life and later wrote about him, and he helped set up the Samajik Samarasata Manch. For a union, this means that caste, language, region and religion must never become a basis for distinguishing between workers.

## What the ideas ask of a karyakarta

It is easy to quote ideas and hard to apply them. A few practical tests follow from the list above.

- Does my union have a written charter of demands, and does it present it with data and arguments?
- Do I treat the employer as someone to negotiate with, and do I still protect the worker without compromise?
- Do contract, casual and self-employed workers have a place in my union, or only permanent employees?
- Am I helping workers to understand their rights and the law, so that they do not depend on rumour?
- Do I treat every worker alike, whatever their caste or region?

A point to note is that Thengadi's ideas are not a ready-made rulebook. They were developed over decades in response to changing conditions, from the first years of independent India to the era of liberalisation. Each generation of karyakartas has to apply them again to its own time, whether that is platform work, contract employment or the new Labour Codes.

## For karyakartas

The best tribute to him is to read what he wrote. The **Dattopant Thengadi Archive** has put much of it online, including books such as *Labour Policy*, *The Third Way* and *The Perspective*, videos of his talks on subjects such as swadeshi and the WTO, and tributes and memoir pieces by colleagues. A study circle that reads one chapter a month, and then discusses how it applies to the local industry, will do more to carry his thought forward than any ceremony.
